item.title: Niger-Des soldats mutins attaquent l'aéroport de Niamey et le palais présidentiel
item.description: Des soldats mutins au Niger ont attaqué samedi dans la matinée l'aéroport et la présidence à Niamey, la capitale du pays, déclenchant une riposte des forces loyalistes, alors que des tirs nourris et des explosions ont été entendus, tandis que la télévision et la radio d'État ont été brièvement mises hors service.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Des soldats mutins au Niger ont attaqué samedi dans la matinée l'aéroport et la présidence à Niamey, la capitale du pays, déclenchant une riposte des forces loyalistes, alors que des tirs nourris et des explosions ont été entendus, tandis que la télévision et la radio d'État ont été brièvement mises hors service. En fin de matinée, le ministère de la Défense du Niger a déclaré que les forces armées reprenaient progressivement le contrôle des sites ciblés, mais des sources sécuritaires ont indiqué que des mutins étaient toujours présents à l'aéroport et que la situation générale restait floue. La télévision et la radio d'État ont été mis hors service à 8 heures du matin, heure locale (8 heures GMT), avant de reprendre par la suite ses programmes. La télévision d'État a notamment diffusé un message indiquant que des soldats mutins d'une base de Niamey avaient ouvert le feu sur des "sites sensibles" dans la ville. Les forces de sécurité ont réagi rapidement et "maîtrisé les troubles", a-t-elle indiqué. C'est la troisième fois depuis le début de l'année que Niamey - et plus précisément le complexe abritant l'aéroport international et une base aérienne militaire – enregistre d'importants troubles. Un climat d'insécurité demeure au Niger depuis la prise du pouvoir par les militaires à la suite d'un coup d'Etat survenu en 2023 qui a porté le général Abdourahamane Tiani à la tête du pays. Ce dernier s'était engagé à améliorer la sécurité dans ce pays du Sahel, important producteur d'uranium, mais les attaques djihadistes persistent. En début d'année, des groupes affiliés à Al Qaïda et à l'Etat islamique ont ainsi mené des attaques contre l'aéroport civil et la base aérienne militaire attenante. L'assaut de samedi a duré des heures et impliqué des soldats des localités d'Ouallam, de Tera et de Dosso, dans le sud-ouest du pays, ont déclaré à Reuters une source sécuritaire nigérienne, ainsi qu'Yvan Guichaoua, chercheur au Centre international d'études des conflits de Bonn. Les troupes déployées dans cette zone ont subi de lourdes pertes lors des combats contre la branche régionale de l'Etat islamique. UNE "ATTAQUE LÂCHE", DÉNONCE UN RESPONSABLE NIGÉRIEN Une autre source sécuritaire avait dans un premier temps rapporté à Reuters que des "terroristes" avaient attaqué l'aéroport international Diori Hamani et tenté de pénétrer au-delà du périmètre de sécurité entourant le palais présidentiel. Un journaliste de Reuters avait également rapporté avoir entendu des tirs nourris aux abords de la présidence aux premières heures de l'aube. À 9h00 GMT, le palais présidentiel semblait avoir été sécurisé par les troupes loyalistes, mais la zone autour de l'aéroport était toujours contestée, ont indiqué deux sources sécuritaires et un diplomate. Deux sources ont indiqué que des troupes loyalistes avaient été dépêchées pour reprendre le contrôle de l'aéroport, soit par la négociation, soit par la force. Selon des analystes et des sources sécuritaires, la frustration envers le gouvernement monte au sein des unités de première ligne. Bana Wagana Ibrahim, membre du Bureau du Niger au sein du Conseil consultatif et député au Parlement de l'Alliance des Etats du Sahel (AES), a déclaré sur Facebook que la Base 101, une importante installation militaire à Niamey, avait été prise pour cible, ajoutant que les forces de sécurité avait repris le contrôle. "Une autre attaque lâche contre la base 101 et encore une fois nos forces de défense et de sécurité ont assuré(...) Situation sous contrôle", a-t-il écrit. Reuters n'a pas été en mesure de vérifier ces informations de manière indépendante. Un porte-parole du gouvernement nigérien n'a pas répondu dans l'immédiat à une demande de commentaires. LE NIGER, PRODUCTEUR CLÉ D'URANIUM Le Niger, pays d'Afrique de l'Ouest riche en minéraux et possédant d'importantes ressources en uranium, en pétrole et en or, est dirigé par des militaires depuis le coup d'État de juillet 2023 qui a renversé le président Mohamed Bazoum. Comme ses voisins le Mali et le Burkina Faso, le Niger fait face à une insurrection armée de groupes djihadistes liés à Al Qaïda et l'Etat islamique et n'est jusqu'ici pas parvenu à inverser la tendance, malgré les promesses des dirigeants militaires d'améliorer la sécurité. La branche ouest-africaine d'Al Qaïda a revendiqué l'attentat perpétré en juin contre l'aéroport de Niamey, cinq mois après que l'Etat islamique au Sahel a ciblé le même site. Le gouvernement d'Abdourahamane Tiani a décidé de tourner le dos aux partenaires occidentaux traditionnels du Niger et d'approfondir ses liens avec la Russie. Il a également rompu ses liens avec le bloc régional de la CEDEAO pour rejoindre le Mali et le Burkina Faso afin de former un bloc dissident. Ces troubles surviennent alors que les autorités nigériennes renforcent leur contrôle sur le secteur de l'uranium, après avoir saisi des actifs du groupe français Orano. Le Niger est un fournisseur clé de combustible nucléaire pour l'Europe, représentant environ 15% de l'approvisionnement en uranium d'Orano à pleine capacité. La semaine dernière, le gouvernement a réattribué les anciens permis d'exploitation d'uranium d'Orano et de GoviEx à des entreprises soutenues par l'Etat, conformément à un décret.

item.title: Une frappe russe sur un entrepôt près de Kyiv provoque une explosion, faisant 37 morts
item.description: Une frappe aérienne russe sur un entrepôt dans la région de Kyiv, survenue dans la nuit de vendredi à samedi, a provoqué une explosion et fait au moins 37 morts, ont indiqué samedi les autorités ukrainiennes.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Une frappe aérienne russe sur un entrepôt dans la région de Kyiv, survenue dans la nuit de vendredi à samedi, a provoqué une explosion et fait au moins 37 morts, ont indiqué samedi les autorités ukrainiennes. Le président ukrainien Volodimir Zelensky à demander des comptes après cette explosion survenue dans un entrepôt, dont le bilan est l'un des plus lourds de ces derniers mois et qui semble être le deuxième incident de ce type en deux mois. "Ceux qui ont laissé cela se produire doivent répondre de leurs décisions", a-t-il écrit sur le réseau social X, ajoutant que des poursuites pénales avaient déjà été ouvertes pour négligence officielle. "La réglementation est en vigueur : les munitions ne peuvent être stockées à proximité des habitations ou d'autres zones résidentielles. Les conclusions qui s'imposent seront certainement tirées", a-t-il ajouté. Des dizaines de personnes ont été blessées et plus de 370 personnes ont été évacuées de la zone de la frappe dans le village de Myla, a déploré le chef de l'Etat ukrainien. Les infrastructures avoisinantes ont subi des "dégâts importants", a-t-il ajouté, notamment des bâtiments résidentiels et un établissement de soins pour personnes âgées. La Russie a intensifié son offensive aérienne contre l'Ukraine, utilisant davantage de missiles balistiques et de drones à réaction difficiles à abattre. Neuf autres régions ukrainiennes ont été visées par des frappes nocturnes menées par la Russie, selon Volodimir Zelensky, notant que la capitale est soumise à des attaques "quasi ininterrompues" de drones à grande vitesse. Des sirènes ont retenti toute la matinée, pour le troisième jour consécutif, l'armée de l'air ukrainienne mettant en garde contre de nouvelles vagues de drones approchant de la capitale. Le chef de l'administration de la région de Kyiv, Tymur Tkachenko, a déclaré qu'une jeune fille de 14 ans avait été tuée samedi lors d'une frappe de drones dans le district de Boryspil. A Kyiv, une fillette de deux ans a été tuée par un drone abattu, a dit pour sa part samedi le maire de la ville, Vitali Klitschko. Les frappes survenues jeudi et vendredi à Kyiv et dans ses environs ont endommagé des entrepôts et des habitations. Certains responsables ukrainiens présentent cette offensive russe comme une campagne visant à "paralyser" la ville. La récente explosion fait suite à un incident similaire survenu le mois dernier à Vyshneve, une ville de la région de Kyiv, où 10 personnes avaient été tuées et des centaines de maisons endommagées après qu'une frappe a déclenché des explosions secondaires. "En cette cinquième année de guerre totale, nous n'avons pas le droit de permettre la répétition de tragédies comme celle qui s'est produite à Vyshneve, et celle survenue dans le district de Boutcha", a écrit sur Telegram le Premier ministre Sergii Koretskyi, qui s'est rendu sur le lieu de l'explosion de vendredi.

item.title: Allianz envisage de racheter le géant de l'assistance routière AA pour £5 mds -Sky News
item.description: L'assureur allemand Allianz envisage de racheter AA, géant britannique de l'assistance routière, pour un montant de 5 milliards de livres sterling (5,84 milliards d'euros), rapporte samedi Sky News.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: L'assureur allemand Allianz (ALVG.DE) envisage de racheter AA, géant britannique de l'assistance routière, pour un montant de 5 milliards de livres sterling (5,84 milliards d'euros), rapporte samedi Sky News. Fondé en 1905 par un groupe de passionnés d'automobile et connue en Grande-Bretagne pour ses dépanneuses de couleur jaune, AA a été introduit en Bourse par ses anciens propriétaires, des fonds d'investissement privés, en 2014, au prix de 250 pence par action, avant d'être retiré de la cote. Allianz fait partie des rares prétendants, aux côtés de la société de capital-investissement EQT, a avoir engagé des discussions avec les conseillers d'AA en vue d'un éventuel un accord, a indiqué Sky News. Les propriétaires d'AA ont étudié depuis le début de l'année deux options pour le groupe, dont une introduction en Bourse à Londres, a précisé la chaîne de télévision. Sollicités, Allianz et AA ont refusé de s'exprimer. Le Financial Times avait rapporté l'année dernière qu'AA envisageait une cession pour 5 milliards de livres sterling et recherchait des acquéreurs.

item.title: Bezzecchi shatters lap record to beat Marquez brothers to Aragon GP pole
item.description: Aprilia's Marco Bezzecchi became the first rider to crack the one minute and 45 seconds barrier at MotorLand, snatching pole position for the Aragon Grand Prix and ending Marc Marquez's bid for a hat-trick of poles at the circuit on Saturday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Aprilia's Marco Bezzecchi became the first rider to crack the one minute and 45 seconds barrier at MotorLand, snatching pole position for the Aragon Grand Prix and ending Marc Marquez's bid for a hat-trick of poles at the circuit on Saturday. The Italian initially set the pace with a time of 1:44.984 before going even faster with another lap record of 1:44.962, leaving Ducati's Marquez unable to match the Aprilia rider's scorching pace. Marquez, who has won seven MotoGP races at Aragon, will start alongside Bezzecchi on the front row despite a heart-stopping moment while braking on a flying lap. His brother Alex Marquez, of Gresini Racing, completes the front row. "Well, it was a positive morning overall... Obviously, the qualifying was good fun. I'm happy to be fast and to grab the pole position," Bezzecchi said. "Now the real job starts... We start in a good place, but Marc and Alex are both super fast in terms of pace with both tyres, so it's going to be a tough fight. But we are enjoying and let's see what we can do." Reigning world champion Marc Marquez accepted that Bezzecchi had the faster bike. "Marco, at the moment, has a better pace than us, so sometimes you cannot do anything. You just try to do your best and it's what we are doing," he said. "I pushed hard on that brake point, maybe too much and I had that moment. I feel that I can keep a constant pace, but Marco basically has a bit faster pace." Trackhouse Racing's Raul Fernandez was fourth-fastest and he will line up on the second row with Aprilia's Jorge Martin and KTM's Pedro Acosta. The third row features VR46 Racing's Fabio Di Giannantonio, Ducati's Francesco Bagnaia and LCR Honda's Johann Zarco, who made a memorable return from a knee injury sustained in a crash at the Catalan Grand Prix in May.

item.title: Bear encounters are on the rise. Here's what to do if you meet one
item.description: If it makes contact, play dead, protecting your head, until it goes away.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: A drought in the western U.S. has devastated wildlands, dried up food sources and sent bears [USN:L6N44M0OO TEXT:"wandering along city sidewalks and into homes and shops"] in search of food. What should you do if you meet a bear? Reuters turned to BearWise , which bear biologists started in the southeastern United States in 2018 and that grew into a national program of the Association of Fish & Wildlife Agencies. SHOULD PEOPLE FEAR BEARS? Over millennia, humans have mythologized, vilified and attributed personalities to bears. Smart, strong and fast, bears can weigh hundreds of pounds and are feared predators in the wild. But they typically avoid people and rarely attack them, scientists say. HOW CAN YOU TELL IF A BEAR FEELS THREATENED? A bear that is huffing, moaning or clacking its jaws is showing it is feeling threatened and prepared to defend itself. BearWise advises standing your ground in the face of a defensive bear, even if it moves toward you. If it makes contact, play dead, protecting your head, until it goes away. WHAT IF THE BEAR IS AGGRESSIVE? While a defensive bear is noisy and obviously stressed, an aggressive or predatory bear is quiet and moves deliberately. In this situation, experts advise shouting, throwing rocks and using bear spray. If a predatory bear makes physical contact, fight back. DOES IT MATTER WHETHER IT'S A BLACK OR GRIZZLY BEAR? No, according to Nate Bowersock, a black bear biologist with the Missouri Department of Conservation and chair of the BearWise working group of the Association of Fish & Wildlife Agencies. The key is to respond to the bear's behavior, not its species. Bears can be hard to tell apart, especially if you are under pressure. Grizzlies, also known as brown bears, are distinguished in appearance by a shoulder hump. Individual black or grizzly bears vary from black to light brown and range in size. WHERE ARE NORTH AMERICA'S BEARS? Black bears are numerous and found across the U.S. and in Canada and Mexico. Most grizzlies, whose population has rebounded because of conservation efforts, live in Alaska and northern Canada, but also in Montana, Wyoming, Idaho and Washington state. HOW CAN YOU AVOID TROUBLE? If you spot a bear, do not approach. Do not gather to gawk if a bear shows up in your neighborhood. If you find a bear in your home or business, leave and call in expert help, Bowersock said. "Back away quietly," he said. Do not feed bears, and that includes not leaving pet food outside, keeping trash bins off the street until pickup morning and keeping barbecue grills clean. IT'S A DROUGHT. SHOULDN'T I FEED THE BEARS? Bowersock said people would be mistaken to think they are helping by feeding bears, and that it is even more important not to do so during a drought. "If a bear finds food near people and starts to associate human areas with food, they will likely spend even more time in the future near people, even during non-drought times."

item.title: Hungry bears wander into US West homes, shops in record numbers
item.description: The driest winter in memory wiped out plants, grasses, berries and nuts that form around 90% of their diet. Their incredible sense of smell is drawing them to human food.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Hay
item.content:encoded: Matt Errico was sitting on the toilet when he heard noises in his Colorado home. The roofer got up and found two young bears about the size of golden retrievers standing in his hallway. After a staring match, they bolted out of the front door. Errico has had bears get into his garbage before but the home invasion earlier this month was a first. “I've definitely never heard of bears inside, you know, cubs inside someone's house,” Errico said of bear encounters in his small mountain town of Granby, about 57 miles (92 km) northwest of Denver. The black bears, also spotted in a Granby vape shop, are among thousands heading into towns and cities across the U.S. West in record numbers. Bears have wandered near a school in Santa Fe, New Mexico, climbed a tree near a farmers market in Denver and startled humans in other ways across the country after the driest winter in memory wiped out plants, grasses, berries and nuts that form around 90% of their diet, according to bear experts and state wildlife agencies. The animals' incredible sense of smell is drawing them to human food. That is leading to record bear deaths in some states as hundreds are euthanized, run over, shot and even electrocuted as they interact with humans, according to wildlife agencies. TESTING THE BEARS With the West's aridification expected to continue, experts fear bears may become habituated to human food and even stop hibernating should winters become too warm and wild food too scarce. “It's like testing the bears in a way that they've never been tested before, and testing humans,” black bear expert Jon Beckmann said. Development has moved people into areas where bears used to forage for food. At the same time, bear populations have rebounded in states like Nevada, where they were largely wiped out over a century ago. Black bears are now the healthiest of the world's eight bear species, with between 17,000 and 20,000 in Colorado alone, according to state authorities. That state is bearing the brunt of encounters after its human population more than doubled in the last 50 years, pushing homes into bear country around cities like Colorado Springs and Vail. Colorado, which only has black bears, has had more than 7,000 sightings in 2026, more than the previous full-year record in 2019, according to the state's wildlife agency. There have been at least six bear attacks in the state. Around 1.5% to 2% of sightings end in euthanization, according to Jonathan Livingston, a spokesperson for Colorado Parks and Wildlife. Bears are typically killed when they are deemed dangerous, such as when they attack humans or break into homes. Conservation groups like the Colorado Bear Coalition say the animals too often pay with their lives for human negligence, and wildlife agencies should do more to prevent conflicts. If people alert authorities to bears early, officials can usually avoid euthanizations by scaring off the animals, Livingston added. Officials and landowners in New Mexico have killed 187 bears this year, the most since 2011, according to the state's wildlife agency, which has relocated 35 adults and 16 cubs. A bear killed a man in New Mexico last week, police reported, marking the state's first fatal attack in 25 years. Utah authorities said they have euthanized 39 animals in 2026, already a record for any full year. In Montana, sightings are too numerous to count, with grizzlies moving into areas they have not visited in decades, the state's wildlife agency said. Twenty-four grizzlies have died this year, most killed after attacking livestock or people or being hit by cars, according to the agency, which did not provide historical data. A man was killed by a grizzly in Montana's Glacier National Park in May. Fatal bear attacks remain rare in the West, with a handful recorded each year. BEARMAGGEDON? Authorities are calling on residents to use bear-resistant garbage bins, not leave trash containers on the street for days and not put pet food or bird seed within reach of the animals. Clashes often begin with dumpster diving and can end with a 200- to 400-pound (91-181 kg) black bear, with 3- to 4-inch (8-10 cm) razor-sharp claws, confronting someone in their kitchen, Livingston said. Nevada bear expert Heather Reich hopes that the animals will find living around humans too stressful and return to the wild, should drought conditions ease. With bears just beginning to put on body weight for hibernation, she fears the encounters will increase. "We can't even imagine what September and October are going to look like. It is going to be just Armageddon for us," said Reich, a former bear manager for Nevada's wildlife agency who now sells electric doormats to deter bears from entering homes.

item.title: US Open 'RedZone' broadcast hopes to replicate NFL TV success
item.description: Tennis fans can keep an eye on 16 courts at once at the year's final Grand Slam as ESPN launches "RedZone at the U.S. Open," a streaming option designed to emulate one of American football's most successful broadcast offerings.
item.dc:creator: Amy Tennery
item.content:encoded: Tennis fans can keep an eye on 16 courts at once at the year's final Grand Slam as ESPN launches "RedZone at the U.S. Open," a streaming option designed to emulate one of American football's most successful broadcast offerings. "RedZone" has been a staple for NFL fans in the U.S. for years, with a multi-hour broadcast shuffling between games to show highlights and live end-zone action without the filler. Amid a growing U.S. appetite for tennis content, domestic U.S. Open broadcaster ESPN is bringing the concept to Flushing Meadows this year from the opening day of the men's and women's singles main draw on August 30 until September 4. A dedicated broadcast team will direct coverage from match to match, keeping a close eye on the household names as well as the lesser-known players on the outer courts in New York. "They'll have access to all 16 courts and all 16 matches that are happening at a given moment," John Suchenski, ESPN's senior director, programming and acquisitions, said. "And they'll make the editorial decisions as to how we move around. "This is all about what are the most important moments in the matches that are happening right now. "So going out to Court 13 with two players that are not as recognisable will likely happen because they may be in a very important point of that match," added Suchenski. "The direction of this offering is to make sure we're getting to the most important point." The programme comes a year after [USN:L4N3TT1W9 TEXT:"ESPN acquired"] the rights to the "RedZone" brand from the NFL in a deal that placed many of the league's media holdings with the network. "It obviously will be unique and different and specific to the U.S. Open but we've drawn inspiration from what the NFL has done so well over the years with the NFL RedZone," Suchenski told Reuters, adding that there would be some advertisements included in the broadcast. The U.S. Open [USN:L2N3OP15C TEXT:"expanded"] in 2025 to an additional day after years of soaring attendances. ESPN signed a deal with the United States Tennis Association in 2024 to continue broadcasting the tournament until 2037.

item.title: US military families ride 'roller coaster of emotions' over six months of Iran war
item.description: The pressures are familiar for the partners and children, mothers and fathers, of American troops. But the suddenness of the conflict and its fitful pace have had a compounding effect, relatives say.
item.dc:creator: Julia Harte
item.content:encoded: Since the United States went to war with Iran six months ago, Courtney Sanders has been helping soldiers’ families fill the gaps left by their loved ones. There are school pickups to coordinate, lost incomes to supplement — and the ever-present separation anxiety. “It's like being on pins and needles all of the time,” Sanders said. She leads the Chicagoland chapter of Blue Star Families, the nation's largest nonprofit serving military families, and her own daughters are in the U.S. Navy. They have served in various overseas locations over the past six months, including the Middle East. The U.S. has more than 50,000 troops stationed across the region and has deployed thousands of additional Marines and sailors to support the war effort. Eighteen U.S. service members [USN:L6N44I0PX TEXT:"have been killed"] in the conflict and more than 750 wounded. During the war's on-and-off fighting, shuttle diplomacy and [USN:L1N44E0F1 TEXT:"failed peace talks"], military families have experienced a “roller coaster of emotions,” Sanders said. “The moment that you feel you're able to take a breath, you get gut-punched again.” These are familiar pressures for the partners and children, mothers and fathers, of American troops. But the suddenness of the Iranian conflict, and its fitful pace, have had a compounding effect, relatives told Reuters. In a Blue Star Families poll of some 200 active-duty military families in early March, 81% reported elevated stress from the Iran conflict. The group has responded by stepping up its programming, creating online resource hubs, hosting webinars and in-person meet-ups, and matching military spouses going through a deployment for the first time with those who have been through it before. Many service members' deployments have been extended unexpectedly. The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier went more than 200 days without a [USN:P8N3S5026 TEXT:"port call"] — a modern-day record, according to Democratic lawmakers — and military outlets reported suicide attempts and declining morale among its 5,000 sailors and Marines. U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the reports “completely misrepresented” the conditions on board. Some military families find themselves in financial straits. National Guard members, for example, often work regular jobs when they are not deployed. The sudden loss of their main paycheck can make it hard for those left behind to keep food on the table, Sanders said. "There is a huge misconception in the civilian world that if you are in the military, all of your bills are taken care of,” she said. “And that is just frankly not true.” In a statement, the Pentagon said: "We see these families (and) we hear their concerns. We will do whatever is necessary to provide the resources, assistance, and stability they need and deserve during these challenging times." 'A LOT OF EMOTIONS' Shannon, an Army spouse and mother of three in North Carolina who requested Reuters use only her first name for security reasons, tries to tune out the news and the political debate surrounding the war. In February, her husband deployed to the region with five days' notice and could only contact her sporadically for the first several months. Although they have maintained near-daily communication since June, "there are a lot of emotions,” Shannon said, “especially when people are dying over there.” Her children started therapy over the summer. She tries to be strong in front of them, but cries sometimes when they’re not around. Soon after her husband's deployment, Shannon joined an Army-sponsored soldier-and-family "readiness group" within her husband's unit, helping organize meal trains and other support for family members in need. "Every day is not going to be a great day, but you've gotta just keep going and keep yourself busy," she said. In Virginia, Pat, a Navy spouse who also asked to be identified by her first name for security reasons, has tried to keep life as normal as possible for her children, who are in middle and high school. Since her husband deployed about five months ago, Pat said, her neighbors have been "amazing" about helping with kid pickups and other chores. Her family wears red on Fridays — a show of support for deployed service members — and so do many of her children's classmates, even those without military connections. Pat's husband has deployed before. She was pleasantly surprised this time to discover his ship had Wi-Fi, making communication easier. Still, her family is grappling with the uncertainty of when he will return. "Having older kids and knowing that dad wasn't there to see those sporting events, some of that's been a little emotional," she said. "But my kids are very resilient."

item.title: The Week in Breakingviews: When fines are fine
item.description: Meta agreed to pay up to $18 bln to resolve claims that it designed Facebook and Instagram to addict children. This week’s update asks whether legal hits and watchdog fines are too small to work. Plus: Prudential walks a fine line in Hong Kong, and US prison stocks have surged.
item.dc:creator: Liam Proud
item.content:encoded: Welcome back! Liam here, filling in for Peter Thal Larsen. Anthropic’s initial public offering [USN:L4N44O1S2 TEXT:"seems close"]. As you read the listing document, keep in mind some lessons from my colleague Karen Kwok’s coverage. To summarise: the Claude developer’s recent growth deceleration is [USN:L6N44F12H TEXT:"no cause"] for panic; its shares could [USN:L6N42414K TEXT:"serve"] as M&A currency; the risks include [USN:L6N41Y0ZA TEXT:"corporate AI"] fatigue, [USN:L6N42M074 TEXT:"governments"] and [USN:L6N4250T1 TEXT:"open-source"] models; and “run-rate” revenue figures are [USN:L6N3ZY167 TEXT:"misleading"]. More to add? Email me . (If this newsletter was forwarded to you, sign up here to get it in your inbox every weekend.) OPENING LINE “How do you know when a hedge fund manager is talking his book? His mouth is moving.” Read more: [USN:L6N44M0TI TEXT:"Beware hedge fund managers trashing US policy"]. FIVE THINGS I LEARNED FROM BREAKINGVIEWS THIS WEEK Alibaba’s AI capex splurge implies a “mid-teens” return on invested capital, Morgan Stanley analysts calculate. ([USN:L6N44L04S TEXT:"Time to deliver"]) U.S. and Canadian cinemas sold $4.4 billion of tickets between May and August 23, about 6% ahead of 2019. ([USN:L6N44L0Q9 TEXT:"Thanks to higher prices"]) Absolut vodka owner Pernod Ricard’s sales fell 19% year-on-year in China in the financial year to June. ([USN:L6N44O0LS TEXT:"Time for a dividend cut"]) Nvidia had struck $70 billion of direct equity investments as of August 17. ([USN:L6N44N16H TEXT:"Plus $230 billion of backstops"]) Unitree and its rival Chinese robot makers may ship 100,000 units this year. ([USN:L6N44O093 TEXT:"But its CEO is not smiling"]) COST OF BUSINESS No CEO wants to be in the position that Mark Zuckerberg found himself in this week. His tech giant Meta Platforms (META.O) on Wednesday [USN:L6N44N0VA TEXT:"agreed"] to pay up to $18 billion to settle claims, made by nearly all U.S. states, that the company designed Facebook and Instagram to keep children addicted to social media. Still, its shares ended the day up 1%, indicating either that investors didn’t care or perhaps that the sum was smaller than they feared. As Jonathan Guilford [USN:L6N44O06H TEXT:"pointed out"], it’s a tiny amount relative to the roughly $80 billion of net income that analysts expect Meta to generate this year. The legal payments are also spread over a decade, which means they’re lower in today’s money than the headline figure suggests. For the sake of simplicity, assume 10 equal installments starting immediately and discounted at a 10% rate. The present value would be $12 billion, or 0.8% of Meta’s almost $1.5 trillion market capitalisation. In India, meanwhile, Shritama Bose [USN:L6N44L0HZ TEXT:"dug into"] a decision by the local regulator to bar a JPMorgan entity and another Mumbai-based broker. It’s part of a [USN:L6N42X0BM TEXT:"wider crackdown"] on what the watchdog sees as market manipulation in the country’s $6 trillion equity derivatives market. The financial penalty in this case? Just a few hundred thousand dollars. That won’t trouble JPMorgan (JPM.N) boss Jamie Dimon much. True, in both cases the real punishment is arguably non-financial. Zuckerberg, for example, pledged meaningful changes to Meta’s apps, including age verification, limiting 14-to-17-year-olds to two hours of usage and restricting night-time notifications. Yet Jonathan is sceptical that these tweaks will amount to much, [USN:L6N44O06H TEXT:"concluding"] that Meta has ultimately paid a small price to secure its industry status. More broadly, it’s notable that fines and other similar penalties don’t seem to have kept pace with soaring stock markets in recent years. Good Jobs First, a non-profit that “promotes corporate and government accountability in economic development”, keeps a database that tracks regulatory punishments and other payouts related to corporate misconduct, including many legal cases like those brought by state attorneys general. Total annual U.S. penalties peaked at $84 billion in 2024, but that figure was not much bigger than the previous high of $81 billion in 2015. For comparison, the total value of the benchmark S&P 500 Index almost tripled over the same period. In other words, the drag to shareholders from corporate misconduct seems to be fading as a percentage of overall market capitalisation. None of this is to say that Zuckerberg can rest easy. He will have a lot of other things on his mind this weekend. Robert Cyran, drawing on a Reuters investigation , on Wednesday [USN:L6N44M10Z TEXT:"examined"] why Meta’s efforts to remake itself around artificial intelligence have run into repeated setbacks. The takeaway is striking. Technological revolutions are always tough for incumbents, and Meta is now one of them. That’s a far bigger problem for the company than a legal bill that failed to dent the share price. CHART OF THE WEEK Beijing has been [USN:L4N42D0HQ TEXT:"tightening"] its [USN:L4N4420RA TEXT:"grip"] on Chinese wealth held outside of the mainland, particularly in [USN:L4N42P0F4 TEXT:"Hong Kong"]. It’s not great news for insurers like [USN:L4N44H0E1 TEXT:"AIA"] and Prudential. Policies bought in the financial centre have long been a popular channel for mainland visitors to diversify their assets offshore. But as Katrina Hamlin [USN:L6N44O007 TEXT:"showed"] in this chart on Thursday, which was published alongside a piece about Prudential’s results, the underlying demand is still strong. And some types of policies seem less vulnerable than others. THE WEEK IN PODCASTS For a long time, the received wisdom among Western economists was that liberal democracy and capitalism go hand in hand. Today, that consensus lies in tatters. On The Big View , economist Daron Acemoglu tells Peter Thal Larsen that the institutions, laws and freedoms that made the West rich are under threat. The Nobel laureate has a plan to change that. Over on the Viewsroom , Aimee Donnellan, Jonathan Guilford and Gabriel Rubin previewed Kevin Warsh’s first Jackson Hole symposium as chair of the Federal Reserve. His strategy of staying tight-lipped on interest rates, and hoping investors will focus on the real economy, may have long-term consequences. PARTING SHOT Of all the so-called Trump trades that rose to prominence at the start of the U.S. president’s second term, prison stocks have been arguably the most enduring. GEO (GEO.N) and CoreCivic (CXW.N) together oversee approximately 165 correctional facilities, with space for roughly 160,000 inmates. As Jeffrey Goldfarb [USN:L6N44A1BM TEXT:"writes"], they’ve trounced the benchmark S&P 500 Index since November 2024, even though violent crime has been falling for years. An enlarged and emboldened Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency is keeping wardens busy, but it doesn’t look politically or financially sustainable. item.title: Manila like a local
item.description: Our bureau chief’s guide to adobo, jeepneys and streetwear.
item.dc:creator: Karen Lema
item.content:encoded:
REUTERS/Illustration/Kate Evans The first things you notice when you arrive in Manila are the traffic, the clinging heat and the constant noise. It can feel overwhelming initially, with streets that rarely seem to slow down. But stay a little longer, and something else begins to emerge. Manila is not just a city of congestion and chaos. It is also a place of warm welcomes, lively street life and food that draws people together. Beneath the frenetic pace is a city shaped by centuries of history, with neighbourhoods still anchored by Spanish churches and cobblestone streets worn down by time and footsteps, where conversations linger and weekend escapes to beaches and mountains are never far away. I was born in the Philippines and have spent two decades covering the country for Reuters — its economic cycles, its political upheavals and its navigation of its place in an increasingly tense region. What emerges is a city that can be rough and uneven, yes, but also layered and beautiful. Here’s how to experience Manila like a local: The way around: I love to cycle, but Manila often has other ideas. This is not a city known for its bike lanes, and public transport can be patchy and unpredictable. You learn to adapt. A jeepney drives through Binondo, the world's oldest Chinatown, in Manila, Philippines, August 24, 2026. REUTERS/Eloisa Lopez The most iconic transport option is the jeepney, a colourful, open-sided minibus also known as the "King of the Road," and a symbol of Filipino ingenuity. They’re cheap and ubiquitous — fares start at around 14 pesos ($0.22), if you don’t mind the heat and sitting shoulder to shoulder with strangers. For more predictable trips, there’s Grab, the ride-hailing app that has become a go-to for many professionals despite the higher cost. The Light Rail Transit and Metro Rail Transit offer a faster way to cut through the traffic , connecting Manila with neighbouring cities in the capital region, though trains can be crowded during peak hours. Things to see: One of the bestplaces to begin your exploration is Intramuros, the old walled city that served as the seat of Spanish colonial power in the heart of the capital. Its centuries-old churches, stone fortifications and cobblestone streets offer a glimpse into Manila's colonial past. People walk along Fort Santiago at Intramuros in Manila, Philippines, August 24, 2026. REUTERS/Eloisa Lopez People sit at Casa Manila in Intramuros, Manila, Philippines, August 24, 2026. REUTERS/Eloisa Lopez From there, continue to Binondo, the world’s oldest Chinatown, where commerce hums alongside a wide array of Chinese dishes, noodle shops, dim sum restaurants, and bakeries selling steamed pork buns, sweet bean-filled pastries and spring rolls in a way that feels both ancient and entirely present. A few streets away stands Quiapo Church , home to the revered "Black Nazarene" statue of Christ, whose annual January procession draws millions of devotees in one of the largest expressions of Catholic faith in Asia. Not far away is Rizal Park, popularly known as Luneta, where the imposing monument to national hero José Rizal — whose writings helped inspire the movement that led to the Philippine Revolution in the 1890s against Spanish rule — stands watch over the city. An ice cream vendor, locally known as Mamang Sorbetero, prepares a cone of ice cream as a girl looks over the ice cream cart at Quiapo. REUTERS/Eloisa Lopez A couple poses for a photo with Juan Luna's Spoliarium in the background at the National Museum of Fine Arts. REUTERS/Eloisa Lopez Across the park lies the National Museum Complex , home to archaeological treasures, ethnographic collections and some of the country's most important works of art, including Juan Luna's "Spoliarium," a monumental 19th-century painting depicting fallen gladiators being dragged from a Roman arena. A couple of kilometres away, overlooking the Pasig River, you'll find Malacañang Palace, the official residence and workplace of the Philippine president, originally built during the Spanish colonial era. For a glimpse of Manila at its most frenetic, head to Divisoria, a sprawling wholesale and retail market packed with malls, street stalls and warehouses. Here, shoppers weave through crowds in search of bargains on everything from clothes and shoes to party supplies, decorations, household goods and gadgets, with goods including low-cost imports and locally made products. The definitive food item: If you’ve spent any time on food shows or travel blogs, you’ve likely come across adobo, the Philippines’ most recognisable dish. At its simplest, it is pork or chicken braised in vinegar, soy sauce, garlic, peppercorns and bay leaves, creating a balance of sour and savoury flavours. It is also forgiving: even someone like me, who rarely cooks, can make a decent adobo. For a restaurant version, many locals swear by Manam 's. Adobo, a Filipino dish of pork and chicken cooked in vinegar, soy sauce, garlic, peppercorns and bay leaves, is served at a branch of Manam restaurant; Balut, a fertilised duck egg with a partially developed embryo, is displayed for sale at a street food cart at Binondo; Vinegar is poured on a plastic cup of duck eggs, locally known as penoy, at a street food stall at Divisoria. REUTERS/Eloisa Lopez Then there is balut, a fertilised duck egg with a partially developed embryo, often eaten straight from the shell on the street. It has appeared on TV shows like “Fear Factor” because of how it looks, but locals see it as a protein-rich snack, best enjoyed warm with salt or vinegar. Even outsiders might be familiar with Jollibee, the homegrown fast-food giant where crispy Chickenjoy, sweet-style spaghetti and peach mango pie have become comfort-food staples across generations. To wash it down, there is fresh coconut juice sold on street corners, scooped straight from the shell and served over ice, with tender coconut meat included. For runners like me, it is the perfect recovery drink. For dessert, try halo-halo, which literally means “mix-mix,” a concoction of sweetened beans, jellies and fruit layered beneath shaved ice, milk, caramel custard and purple yam. My personal favourite is found at Razon's , whose pared-down version proves that less can sometimes be more. Others recommend Bebang's , which uses frozen milk instead of shaved ice. Beneath the frenetic pace is a city shaped by centuries of history, with neighbourhoods still anchored by Spanish churches and cobblestone streets worn down by time and footsteps, where conversations linger and weekend escapes to beaches and mountains are never far away. Dress like a local: In Manila’s heat and humidity, breathable fabrics are essential. Cotton remains a reliable choice and on any given day you will see cotton shirts paired with shorts or loose trousers, although many locals have also embraced modern technical textiles. Local brands BENCH/ and Penshoppe are everywhere, offering affordable everyday clothing. Footwear tends toward the practical — I usually opt for sneakers, which are best for Manila’s uneven sidewalks. If you really want to fit in, carry an umbrella — useful as much for shade as for the sudden downpours. Getting away: A two- or three-hour drive out of the city takes you to beaches, mountains and cooler air. In Batangas, 66 miles (107 km) south of Manila, the water clears and the pace slows. Diving spots around Anilao attract everyone from beginners to seasoned divers for their vibrant coral reefs and sea turtles. One of its best-known sites is The Cathedral, which features an underwater cross surrounded by reef fish. Or head to Tagaytay, perched on a ridge overlooking Taal Volcano — one of the world’s smallest active volcanoes, which sits on an island in the middle of a lake. The city has become a food destination, known for bulalo, a rich beef marrow soup, tawilis, a freshwater sardine found only in Taal Lake, and buko (coconut) pie, a regional staple. Cafes make the most of the breeze. For something more active, hike up Mount Makiling, a volcano steeped in folklore, or ride the rapids at Pagsanjan Falls. CITY MEMO DATA POINTS Population: 1.9 million Price of a cup of coffee: 15 pesos ($0.24) for a black coffee from a roadside stall, poured from a thermos. For something a step up but distinctly Filipino, head to Bo’s Coffee , which champions local beans, or Figaro , a long-time fixture of the café scene. Newer chains such as But First, Coffee reflect how quickly Manila’s coffee culture is evolving, with most drinks costing less than 300 pesos ($4.50). Price of an ice cream scoop: 10-20 pesos ($0.16-0.32) for a scoop from roaming ice cream vendors pushing colourful carts and referred to as Mamang Sorbetero. The name comes from sorbetes, a traditional Filipino frozen dessert, and “mamang,” a familiar way of referring to an older man. They sell coconut-based ice cream, churned the old-fashioned way and served in flavours such as cheese, chocolate, ube and mango. For something more artisan, Manila Creamery offers Filipino-inspired flavours such as ube, tablea and durian for 120-160 pesos ($1.95-$2.60) per scoop. Great place to see a sunset: Manila Bay — sitting at a café on Roxas Boulevard, walking the bay front, or looking out from a hotel balcony. Oldest university: University of Santo Tomas, founded in 1611 and now home to more than 40,000 students.

item.title: Chopra ends season early after ligament tear
item.description: Former Olympic champion Neeraj Chopra has ended his 2026 season early after sustaining a ligament tear during training, the javelin thrower announced in an Instagram post on Saturday, three weeks before the Asian Games.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Former Olympic champion Neeraj Chopra has ended his 2026 season early after sustaining a ligament tear during training, the javelin thrower announced in an Instagram post on Saturday, three weeks before the Asian Games. The 28-year-old Indian, who took gold at the Tokyo Olympics and won silver in Paris, placed second in the Lausanne Diamond League with a throw of 88.05 metres last week, but suffered the injury soon after, getting sidelined for a long period for the second time in a year. "After discussions with my doctor and team, we've decided that I will sit out the rest of this season," Chopra posted. "It's disappointing, especially because I felt close to finding my rhythm. But as they say, setbacks are a part of the journey." Chopra, who was dealing with lower back discomfort since 2023, aggravated a disc injury in September 2025 during training. He went into a nine-month rehabilitation period after the Tokyo World Championships, and returned in June. He had qualified for the Diamond League finals next week, and was a medal hope for India at next month's Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games. "My focus now is on recovering well and coming back even stronger," Chopra added.

item.title: Russian strike on Kyiv-area ammunition depot triggers blast, killing 37
item.description: At least 37 people were killed after a Russian drone attack on a Kyiv-area ammunition depot sparked a detonation, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Saturday, vowing to punish suspected negligence in the second such incident in two months.
item.dc:creator: Dan Peleschuk
item.content:encoded: At least 37 people were killed after a Russian drone attack on a Kyiv-area ammunition depot sparked a detonation, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Saturday, vowing to punish suspected negligence in the second such incident in two months. The deadliest Russian strike in the Kyiv area this year came as Moscow's air attacks on the Ukrainian capital and surrounding region dragged into a third straight day, killing residents, damaging homes and derailing daily life. Dozens were also injured and hundreds evacuated from the area of the strike late on Friday on the village of Myla, Zelenskiy said, where nearby infrastructure including residential buildings and a facility for the elderly and people with disabilities suffered "significant damage". The attack sparked widespread fires, officials said. Among those killed was the head of a neighbouring village who rushed to help. "A terrible situation and terrible negligence on the part of those who stored explosives right next to people," Zelenskiy said in a video address. SECOND STRIKE-RELATED DETONATION IN TWO MONTHS The site of Friday's blast was a military facility that held artillery shells, mines and drones, among other ammunition, he added. It followed [USN:L1N43705J TEXT:"a similar incident"] in the Kyiv-area town of Vyshneve last month, when 10 people were killed and hundreds of houses damaged after a strike triggered secondary explosions. "Another such crime – after what happened in Vyshneve – is absolutely unacceptable," Zelenskiy said. "I expect the details to be presented to the public promptly." He added that criminal cases had already been opened on charges of official negligence. Ukrainian officials rarely disclose damage to military targets from Russian attacks. In a statement on Saturday, Ukraine's Defence Ministry said all those responsible for weapons storage should complete a full audit of their locations. DRONE SWARMS GRIP KYIV FOR DAYS Nine other regions had been targeted in overnight strikes by Russia, Zelenskiy added, saying Kyiv in particular was under "virtually non-stop attack" from jet-powered drones. Russia has [USN:L8N42A0SA TEXT:"escalated its air war"] on Ukraine with increasing numbers of elusive ballistic missiles and new high-speed drones, which Kyiv lacks the air defences to shoot down. On Saturday, sirens blared throughout the morning and afternoon for a third straight day as Ukraine's air force warned of new waves of drones approaching the capital. The sound of air defences boomed across the sky. Kyiv region governor Tymur Tkachenko said a 14-year-old girl was killed in a morning drone strike on the Boryspil district. In Kyiv, a 2-year-old girl was killed by a downed drone, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Saturday. Strikes in and around the city on Thursday and Friday had damaged residential buildings and storage facilities belonging to major retailers, part of what some Ukrainian officials said was [USN:L1N44P057 TEXT:"a campaign aimed at"] "paralysing" the city of several million.

item.title: German insurer Allianz weighs $6.77 billion takeover of AA roadside rescue giant, Sky News reports
item.description: Germany-based financial services company Allianz is considering a £5 billion ($6.77 billion) takeover swoop for AA, the breakdown recovery group, Sky News reported on Saturday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Germany-based financial services company Allianz (ALVG.DE) is considering a £5 billion ($6.77 billion) takeover swoop for AA, the breakdown recovery group, Sky News reported on Saturday. AA, founded by a group of motoring enthusiasts in 1905 and known in Britain for its yellow recovery vehicles, was taken public by its previous private equity owners in 2014 at 250 pence a share. Allianz is one of a small number of parties which have been holding talks with advisers to the AA about a deal, Sky News said, adding that private equity firm EQT was another bidder. The AA's private equity owners have been pursuing a so-called dual-track process for most of this year, with the alternative to a sale being a public listing on the London Stock Exchange, Sky News said. Both companies declined to comment. The Financial Times reported last year that the British roadside recovery company was eyeing a £5 billion sale and was seeking buyers. ($1 = 0.7390 pounds)

item.title: Norris extends to 2030 and would be happy to end career at McLaren
item.description: Formula One world champion Lando Norris announced a contract extension with McLaren until at least the end of 2030 on Saturday, and said he would be happy to see out his career with a team that felt like home.
item.dc:creator: Alan Baldwin
item.content:encoded: Formula One world champion Lando Norris announced a contract extension with McLaren until at least the end of 2030 on Saturday, and said he would be happy to see out his career with a team that felt like home. The 26-year-old Briton, winner of the last two races in Hungary and the Netherlands, broke the news to McLaren employees at a friends and family day at the Woking factory. McLaren said there was also a multi-year option to commit beyond 2030, and Norris had been gifted an MCL39 car from last season when he became the team's first drivers' champion since Lewis Hamilton in 2008. Speaking earlier to reporters, Norris said the deal came at a perfect time for team morale and motivation, but the figures seen in some media speculation were wide of the mark. "At the minute there's really no reason to want to even put a thought into somewhere else," he said. "I kind of want my whole career to be with McLaren because I'm happy here and I don't want to change. "I want to fight with McLaren even when things are not going well and I want to win with McLaren when things are going amazingly well. So yeah, I'll be very, very happy at the end of my career to say that McLaren was the only team I've been with." Norris made his McLaren F1 debut in 2019, after joining in 2017 as a test and simulator driver, and has now won 13 grands prix with the reigning constructors' champions, as well as 18 poles. "This extension gives us important continuity and reinforces our confidence in the direction we are taking together," said team principal Andrea Stella. "With him and Oscar (Piastri), we know we can count not only on one of the strongest partnerships but also on one of the most united and close-knit teams in Formula One.” MORE MONEY BUT NOT AS MUCH AS VERSTAPPEN AND HAMILTON Some media reports have suggested the new deal would put the Briton third in Formula One's pay rankings, behind only Red Bull's Max Verstappen and Ferrari's Hamilton. One speculated that Norris's new salary could be around €60 million ($69.6 million) a year. "I feel like I should earn as much as that," he grinned in response to a mention of what four-time champion Verstappen and seven-time champion Hamilton might be on. "But it's certainly not close to the figures that I've been seeing online, sadly... of course it's a bit more, as it is with any job when you kind of extend and do those things, but it's certainly not close to the level of Lewis or Max, which in a way it shouldn't be, because I've not achieved as much as what they've achieved in their careers. "I'm working on it, you know. I don't know when my next extension or renewal would be and hopefully I can then try and match it one day. I dream of seeing those figures that I've seen online so I'll keep dreaming of them one day." Norris said there had been some interest from other teams, but none expressed towards them, and it would have felt like a betrayal to go anywhere else. "Really it was quite the easiest decision I've had to make in my career so far," he said.

item.title: Caitlin Clark, Kelsey Mitchell combine for 68 as Fever trounce Sun
item.description: Caitlin Clark and Kelsey Mitchell each scored 34 points, carrying the Indiana Fever past the Connecticut Sun for a 111-91 runaway on Friday night in Indianapolis.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Caitlin Clark and Kelsey Mitchell each scored 34 points, carrying the Indiana Fever past the Connecticut Sun for a 111-91 runaway on Friday night in Indianapolis. Clark, who distributed 12 assists, and Mitchell both shot 12-for-19 from the field. Clark connected on 6 of 12 3-point shots, while Mitchell went 4 of 9 from long distance. Aliyah Boston provided 14 points for Indiana, which overcame a shoddy opening stretch of the game. Makayla Timpson tacked on 10 points and eight rebounds for the Fever (26-14), who have won seven of their past nine games. Diamond Miller recorded 19 points while rookie Nell Angloma tallied a season-high 17 points off the bench for Connecticut. Aaliyah Edwards and reserve Hailey Van Lith both added 12 points. The Sun (10-29) began a three-game road trip with their fourth loss in a five-game stretch. They shot 9-for-28 (32.1%) from 3-point range. Indiana reached the 100-point mark for the third consecutive game. The Fever outscored the Sun 21-12 on free throws. Indiana ended up making 39 of 67 shots from the floor (58.2%), while Connecticut made 35 of 76 (46.1%). Connecticut was within 67-57 in the third quarter before the Fever closed the period on a 9-0 spurt. After a slow start, the Fever built a 58-43 halftime lead, buoyed by a 39-15 scoring advantage in the second quarter. Clark had 18 points while Mitchell had 17 at the break. Indiana made one of its first eight attempts from 3-point range but then connected five times on its next seven long-range launches. The Fever held a 24-12 rebounding edge in the first half. The Sun built a 28-14 lead in the first quarter behind Miller's 12 points. The Fever scored the last five points of the quarter but made only four of 14 shots from the floor in the period overall. Indiana won all three regular-season games vs. the Sun this season. --Field Level Media

item.title: Liverpool finalise agreement to sign PSG's Barcola in deal worth up to £123 million, reports say
item.description: Liverpool have finalised an agreement to sign French forward Bradley Barcola from European champions Paris St Germain in a deal worth up to £123 million ($166.43 million), media reports said on Saturday, with the 23-year-old set to become the latest high-profile addition to Andoni Iraola's squad.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Liverpool have finalised an agreement to sign French forward Bradley Barcola from European champions Paris St Germain in a deal worth up to £123 million ($166.43 million), media reports said on Saturday, with the 23-year-old set to become the latest high-profile addition to Andoni Iraola's squad. The 20-times English champions will pay a package worth £106 million, with add-ons potentially rising to £17 million, for Barcola, the BBC said. The Athletic reported that he is set to sign a five-year contract. Reuters has contacted Liverpool and PSG for comment. Barcola joined PSG from his boyhood club Olympique Lyonnais in 2023 and went on to enjoy a trophy-laden spell in the French capital, winning back-to-back Champions League titles in 2024-25 and 2025-26, three Ligue 1 crowns and two French Cups, among other honours. He made 152 appearances across all competitions for PSG, scoring 39 goals and supplying 37 assists. He had two years remaining on his PSG contract. Barcola would be the latest addition to [USN:L1N42C0TK TEXT:"new manager Andoni Iraola"]'s squad following the close-season arrivals of Uruguayan defender [USN:L1N4470P0 TEXT:"Ronald Araujo"] on loan, French centre back Jeremy Jacquet and Spanish forward [USN:L4N42Q1LJ TEXT:"Victor Munoz"]. Liverpool's attacking options currently include British record signing [USN:L4N3UJ0YF TEXT:"Alexander Isak"], Cody Gakpo, Rio Ngumoha and Munoz as the Merseyside club adjusts to life after talisman [USN:L1N40C15L TEXT:"Mohamed Salah"]'s departure. Forward [USN:L1N40Y0UY TEXT:"Hugo Ekitike"] is also sidelined with a long-term injury. Liverpool host Nottingham Forest later on Saturday. ($1 = 0.7390 pounds)

item.title: MLB roundup: Dodgers prevail in Tarik Skubal's return to Detroit
item.description: Freddie Freeman drove in the go-ahead run during the eighth inning in Tarik Skubal's return to Detroit as the Los Angeles Dodgers edged the slumping Tigers 2-1 on Friday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Freddie Freeman drove in the go-ahead run during the eighth inning in Tarik Skubal's return to Detroit as the Los Angeles Dodgers edged the slumping Tigers 2-1 on Friday. Skubal gave up one run on four hits while striking out seven in six innings. The two-time Cy Young Award winner was dealt by the Tigers to the Dodgers earlier this month. Evan Phillips (2-2) struck out all three batters he faced and earned the win, and Tanner Scott pitched the ninth for his 20th save. Miguel Rojas drove in the other Los Angeles run with a pinch-hit single in the sixth as the Dodgers snapped a three-game losing streak. Detroit starter Drew Anderson held the Dodgers, who left 15 men on base, scoreless over 4 2/3 innings despite giving up four hits and walking five. Max Clark's triple knocked in the lone run for the Tigers, who took their eighth loss in nine games. Phillies 5, Angels 3 Pinch hitter Edmundo Sosa hit a go-ahead grand slam with two outs in the top of the ninth inning as Philadelphia rallied past Los Angeles in Anaheim, Calif. Angels reliever Sammy Peralta entered with the bases loaded to face Sosa, who delivered his first career grand slam. Luis Arraez and Kyle Schwarber each had two hits for the Phillies, who won for the 11th time in 13 games. Wade Meckler went 1-for-3 with a walk, an RBI, a run and a homer-saving catch for the Angels, who took their fifth straight loss. Yankees 1, Red Sox 0 Cam Schlittler withstood five walks in 5 2/3 innings and Yankees outfielders started a pair of double plays during New York's victory over visiting Boston. Paul Goldschmidt homered off Boston starter Patrick Sandoval (1-3) in the third inning. Schlittler (12-6) allowed two hits, struck out eight and lowered his AL-leading ERA to 2.09. David Bednar recorded a 1-2-3 ninth for his 31st save. Sandoval gave up one run on three hits over 5 1/3 innings as the Red Sox took their second loss in a row. Reds 10, Cubs 8 Tyler Stephenson belted a three-run homer and Sal Stewart drove in two runs to set the franchise rookie record for RBIs in a season, fueling visiting Cincinnati to a victory over Chicago. Stewart went deep in the fifth inning for his team-leading 29th homer of the season. It also marked his 101st RBI, snapping a tie for the franchise rookie record that Jim Greengrass set in 1953. Cincinnati scored 10 runs for the second straight game to make a winner out of Rhett Lowder (6-8), who allowed three runs in five innings. Pedro Ramirez belted a three-run homer, Michael Busch hit a two-run shot and Seiya Suzuki joined Nico Hoerner in collecting three hits apiece for the Cubs, who have lost six of their past eight games. Brewers 6, Rangers 1 Logan Henderson was nearly perfect for host Milwaukee, which beat Texas for its third straight win. Henderson (9-2) faced 22 batters over seven innings, with Danny Jansen's third-inning homer the only blemish on his stat line. He struck out seven while tying his career high in innings pitched. Christian Yelich finished 3-for-5 for the Brewers, and William Contreras drove in three while going 2-for-4. Cody Bradford (0-3) yielded three runs on nine hits in 5 2/3 innings as the Rangers took their third loss in a row. Royals 3, Guardians 0 Michael Wacha struck out 10 over eight innings and Carter Jensen hit a two-run homer in the ninth, sending red-hot Kansas City to a victory at Cleveland. Wacha (8-8) allowed four singles and did not issue a walk in tying his longest start of the season. He only permitted one runner to get past first base over 103 pitches. The right-hander powered Kansas City to its 11th win in 12 games. The Guardians had their seven-game winning streak snapped. Cleveland starter Tanner Bibee (5-14) tied the Baltimore Orioles' Shane Baz for the major league lead in losses, giving up one run on seven hits in six innings. Astros 3, Mets 1 Hunter Brown struck out a season-high 10 over 6 2/3 solid innings as visiting Houston beat New York. Daulton Varsho had the go-ahead two-run single in the sixth as the Astros won for the third time in four games. Brown (4-3) yielded one run on five hits, and Josh Hader notched his 20th save with a 1-2-3 ninth. Christian Scott (4-4) gave up three runs on one hit and five walks in 5 1/3 innings as the Mets dropped their third game in a row. White Sox 7, Twins 4 Colson Montgomery went 2-for-4 with a homer and three RBIs as Chicago recorded a win over Minnesota in Minneapolis. Andrew Benintendi finished 2-for-4 with a double and two RBIs for the White Sox, who won their third straight game. Grant Taylor (7-2) pitched 2 2/3 scoreless innings of relief, and Bryan Hudson tossed a scoreless ninth for his sixth save. Brooks Lee and Kody Clemens each homered and singled for the Twins, and Walker Jenkins had a hit and a walk in his big-league debut. Dean Kremer (2-5) allowed six runs (five earned) on seven hits over four-plus innings. Braves 6, Rockies 4 Michael Harris II homered, doubled and drove in three runs, Ronald Acuna Jr. added three hits and three runs, and host Atlanta beat Colorado. Mauricio Dubon and Sean Murphy each had two hits and an RBI to back five solid innings by Atlanta starter Grant Holmes (9-5). The right-hander allowed three runs on eight hits for the Braves, who have won five in a row. Raisel Iglesias got the final three outs for his 29th save. Hunter Goodman had three hits and an RBI while Zac Veen and Mickey Moniak had two hits apiece for Colorado, which fell to 2-3 on its seven-game road trip. Rockies starter Tomoyuki Sugano (12-8) allowed six runs on 10 hits over four-plus innings. Cardinals 4, Pirates 1 Rookie Quinn Mathews pitched effectively into the sixth inning for his first major league victory and Jimmy Crooks hit a two-run homer for St. Louis, which beat visiting Pittsburgh. Jordan Walker added three hits and scored twice for the Cardinals, who had lost five of six. Mathews (1-2) allowed a run on five hits over 5 2/3 innings. Ryne Stanek pitched a perfect ninth for his second save. Jared Jones (2-6) permitted three runs on seven hits in 4 1/3 innings for the Pirates, who committed three errors. Pittsburgh has scored a total of five runs in the past five games. Blue Jays 8, Mariners 1 George Springer went 4-for-4 with a solo homer as Toronto defeated visiting Seattle. Nathan Lukes and Kazuma Okamoto added solo shots for the Blue Jays. Okamoto had three RBIs. Dylan Cease (9-5) allowed one run, four hits and one walk while striking out eight in six innings as Toronto earned just its second win in five games. Dominic Canzone stroked a solo homer for the Mariners while going 2-for-4. Randy Arozarena had a single and two walks as Seattle took its second loss in a row. Emerson Hancock (7-8) was tagged for five runs on eight hits in five innings. Nationals 9, Marlins 2 Brady House smacked a three-run homer while Jackson Kent pitched seven innings of one-run ball to earn his first major league win as Washington beat visiting Miami. Harry Ford also homered and Abimelec Ortiz had two hits for the Nationals, who have won consecutive games for the first time since a three-game run Aug. 7-9. Kent (1-2) gave up three hits, walked four and struck out three while throwing 106 pitches. Heriberto Hernandez homered for the Marlins, who had won eight straight games against the Nationals. Eury Perez (7-10) surrendered five runs on two hits in three innings. Rays 9, Padres 4 Yandy Diaz went 2-for-5 with a home run and two RBIs for Tampa Bay, which produced a five-run fourth inning to breeze past San Diego in St. Petersburg, Fla. Chandler Simpson went 2-for-4 with a double, two runs and two stolen bases for the Rays. Cedric Mullins homered, scored twice and drove in two runs. Shane McClanahan (10-6) pitched 5 2/3 innings and allowed four runs, three earned, on three hits. Jackson Merrill went 2-for-3, stroked a two-run homer, walked and scored twice for the Padres. Casey Mize (5-8) surrendered seven runs, two earned, on six hits over five innings. Orioles 4, Athletics 3 (10 innings) Coby Mayo and Christian Encarnacion-Strand each singled home a run in the 10th inning as Baltimore beat the Athletics in West Sacramento, Calif. Brandon Young tossed seven innings of one-run ball for the Orioles, who won for the third time in four games. Andrew Kittredge (3-3) pitched a scoreless ninth inning, and Alex Hoppe allowed a run in the 10th but logged his first career save. The A's, who had won four of their previous five games, got a homer from Jonah Heim. Brady Basso (0-1) yielded the decisive runs in the 10th. Diamondbacks 10, Giants 6 Lars Nootbaar hit the first pitch of the game for a home run, Corbin Carroll and Tim Tawa went deep in a five-run third inning, and visiting Arizona overpowered San Francisco. Nootbaar collected three hits for the Diamondbacks, who moved within a half-game of the National League's third and final wild-card spot. The Diamondbacks bullpen threw five innings and allowed just one unearned run and one hit, with Gerardo Carrillo (3-1) getting the win. Bryce Eldridge and Christian Koss launched homers for the Giants, who took their ninth loss in 11 meetings with Arizona this season. Blade Tidwell (0-1) went five innings, allowing six runs on seven hits. --Field Level Media

item.title: Lower Saxony premier urges agreement on VW restructuring before board meeting
item.description: One of the main players in a struggle to agree a restructuring plan for Volkswagen AG , Lower Saxony state Premier Olaf Lies, said there was heavy pressure on all sides to reach an agreement in the next few days.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: One of the main players in a struggle to agree a restructuring plan for Volkswagen AG , Lower Saxony state Premier Olaf Lies, said there was heavy pressure on all sides to reach an agreement in the next few days. The supervisory board of Europe's largest automaker is due to meet on September 4 to [USN:L8N44O1C5 TEXT:"discuss a turnaround plan"] potentially involving tens of thousands of additional job losses. The issue has pitted VW's management against unions and the German state, its second-biggest shareholder. "I strongly urge that we use the time remaining until the next meeting to bring the different positions together," he told a briefing with journalists on Friday. He said the business challenges facing Volkswagen, which has struggled in the face of costly tariffs, falling demand and mounting competition from China, needed to be handled urgently. But he said the group's position in the wider industrial landscape also had to be considered. "With its sites in Lower Saxony and across Germany, its tens of thousands of employees and their families, and its suppliers and service providers, Volkswagen also bears an enormous responsibility for the wider economy and society," he said. VW Chief Executive Oliver Blume [USN:L8N44M0FW TEXT:"wants to double"] planned job cuts to as many as 50,000, possibly close factories and spin off some company divisions in a radical drive to slash costs across the group. That has triggered fierce opposition from unions and strong concern from Lower Saxony, which has an effective blocking minority shareholding. The two sides are seeking a compromise likely to centre on the scale of job cuts and future plans for factories that are at risk, according to sources familiar with the discussions. "I am convinced that we must find a viable solution here," Lies said. He said VW had always combined economic prudence with social responsibility, "and the solution we are now seeking should be measured against that standard." VW's executive committee, which includes VW's works council chief, as well as Lies and members of the Porsche and Piech shareholder families, is set to convene on Thursday, a day ahead of the supervisory board meeting, to see where things stand.

item.title: L'Iran affirme que la diplomatie et la défense sont indissociables

item.title: Alcaraz says uncertainty over comeback fuelled 'intrusive thoughts'
item.description: Seven-times Grand Slam champion Carlos Alcaraz said "intrusive thoughts" about the timing of his return were the toughest part of a wrist injury layoff that sidelined him for nearly five months ahead of his U.S. Open title defence.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Seven-times Grand Slam champion Carlos Alcaraz said "intrusive thoughts" about the timing of his return were the toughest part of a wrist injury layoff that sidelined him for nearly five months ahead of his U.S. Open title defence. The 23-year-old Spaniard, who became the youngest man to complete the career Grand Slam when he claimed his seventh major title at this year's Australian Open, returns to Flushing Meadows with limited match practice but familiar expectations as he chases a third title in New York. Alcaraz missed most of the clay season and was also forced to sit out the French Open, Wimbledon and the North American hardcourt swing due to the injury. He made his competitive return earlier this week in the U.S. Open mixed doubles alongside 23-times singles Grand Slam champion Serena Williams. "The first month was kind of difficult for me because I couldn't do anything with my right arm. It was tough," Alcaraz told reporters on Friday. "But at the same time, I enjoyed my time with family, friends and staying at home. "But once I started to practice a little bit, that I didn't know when I'm going to start, that thoughts are really difficult to deal with, because I don't know if I'm going to be ready for Cincinnati, for U.S. Open, or I'm going to miss the whole American swing. "But finally, here we are. My goal was try to be healthy as soon as possible and try not to miss more competitions. So I would say that intrusive thoughts were the most difficult things to deal with in this process." The second seed opens his campaign against Russia's Roman Safiullin, ranked 98th in the world, and could face either Arthur Fils or Ben Shelton in the quarter-finals before a potential semi-final clash with 24-times Grand Slam champion Novak Djokovic, 2021 U.S. Open champion Daniil Medvedev, Frances Tiafoe or Brandon Nakashima. The tournament will also be missing world number one Jannik Sinner, Alcaraz's biggest rival, after the 25-year-old Italian withdrew with a persistent right knee injury. "We are not going to see each other for about six months or seven months now. So it's kind of a weird situation," Alcaraz said. "I just wish him all the best. Hopefully a really great recovery and see him back on court at his best once again..." The U.S. Open men's and women's singles main draws get under way on Sunday.

item.title: Norway mourns King Harald as crowds gather at royal palace
item.description: Thousands of Norwegians gathered on Saturday to say goodbye to King Harald in front of the royal palace, where he lies in state, with many well-wishers remembering his sense of inclusiveness and tolerance.
item.dc:creator: Nerijus Adomaitis, Janis Laizans
item.content:encoded: Thousands of Norwegians gathered on Saturday to say goodbye to King Harald in front of the royal palace, where he lies in state, with many well-wishers remembering his sense of inclusiveness and tolerance. Europe's oldest monarch, who emerged from the shadow of his well-loved, extrovert father to become a reformer during more than three decades on the throne, [USN:L6N44P0J6 TEXT:"died on Friday"] at the age of 89. Late on Friday, throngs lined the streets of Oslo in pouring rain to watch the funeral cortege travel from Oslo University Hospital, where Harald died, to the royal palace. Flags were flying at half-mast throughout the country and portraits of the late king in gala uniform were everywhere, from bus stops, trams and metro stations to shops, offices and public buildings. As the nation mourned Harald, attention also turned to the succession. Crown Prince Haakon, the late king's only son, automatically became king upon his father's death under Norway's constitutional monarchy. [USN:L8N3H10JJ TEXT:"King Haakon VIII"] will speak to the nation in a televised address at 1900 local time (1700 GMT) on Saturday. On Tuesday, he [USN:L8N3IG0RD TEXT:"will take the oath"] in front of parliament, when he will swear to defend Norway's constitution and laws. He became king the moment his father passed away. There will be no coronation as they were abolished by parliament in 1908. TOLERANCE AND INCLUSIVENESS The main avenue in central Oslo, Karl Johan, was tightly packed with Norwegians of all walks of life heading towards the palace, clutching flowers, handwritten cards, drawings and small national flags. On what should have been the 58th wedding anniversary of Harald and Queen Sonja, who survives him, they praised the late king's spirit of inclusiveness. "He meant a lot to us immigrants ... We felt really very included. So, thanks to him, I feel so Norwegian," Veselina Vitanova, a 43-year-old teacher originally from Bulgaria, told Reuters outside the palace. Another referred to a speech Harald delivered in 2016 that went viral worldwide, in which he said: "Norwegians are girls who love girls, boys who love boys and girls and boys who love each other". "It embodies the way he felt about people and the way he wanted us Norwegians to feel about each other," said Mari Eidsvaag, 32, who wore a T-shirt emblazoned with that sentence, a rainbow and a drawing of King Harald. "I think it's a very important statement, especially these days," she told Reuters.

item.title: Leao bids emotional farewell to Milan amid reports of Galatasaray switch
item.description: Portugal winger Rafael Leao bid an emotional farewell to AC Milan amid reports he is close to joining Turkish side Galatasaray, saying the decision was difficult but that he would always remain part of the Rossoneri's history.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Portugal winger Rafael Leao bid an emotional farewell to AC Milan amid reports he is close to joining Turkish side Galatasaray, saying the decision was difficult but that he would always remain part of the Rossoneri's history. A product of Sporting Portugal's academy, the 27-year-old has been capped 49 times by his country and represented Portugal at the 2022 and 2026 World Cups. He joined Milan from French side Lille in 2019. Leao became a key figure for the seven-time European champions, scoring 80 goals and providing 65 assists in 291 appearances across all competitions. He helped Milan win the Serie A title in 2021-22 and the Italian Super Cup in the 2024-25 season. According to media reports, Milan have accepted a €45 million ($52.12 million) offer from Galatasaray for Leao, whose contract with the Italian club runs until June 2028. "It's a difficult time," Leao told Sky Sport Italy on Friday after Milan's 2-0 Serie A win over Venezia at the San Siro, where he was not part of the squad. "I've said goodbye to my teammates after seven years. "Milan helped me grow and understand what top-flight football is all about. The time has come to say goodbye. I might have liked to say goodbye in a different way. The fans supported me even during the tough times. "I know what I've achieved here; I'll go down in the club's history. All I can do is say thank you." Milan appointed former Manchester United coach [USN:L6N42O13Y TEXT:"Ruben Amorim"] as manager in June after a disappointing campaign last season that saw them miss out on Champions League qualification. They have since made a strong start to the new Serie A season, winning their opening two matches. "My love for Milan will never end; even from afar, I'll always be watching them...," Leao added. "There are times when you have to make a decision and choose a different path. "Today, Milan showed great quality and have a great manager. He's someone who can help Milan win major trophies. It's the sort of football I like... "Life doesn't end here. I cried; I was moved." ($1 = 0.8634 euros)

item.title: Risk of lake burst near China-Nepal disaster site wanes
item.description: Satellite images suggest that water is slowly flowing out.
item.dc:creator: Liz Lee, Yukun Zhang
item.content:encoded: The threat of a lake formed after a glacier collapse bursting near the China-Nepal border, where a devastating flood struck earlier this week, has eased, Chinese authorities said on Saturday, as it appears to have shrunk.
